Write a compact surface X as U/G by universal-cover classification. If U is the sphere, every nonidentity Möbius map has a fixed point, contradicting the free deck action; G is trivial, so X is the genus-zero sphere. If U=C, the preceding lattice lemma makes X a complex torus of genus one. If U=D, compactness makes G nontrivial. A nonidentity deck automorphism is fixed-point-free in D, hence in its Möbius normal form is hyperbolic (two boundary fixed points) or parabolic (one). To exclude genus zero, its topological sphere has trivial fundamental group, so the universal-cover deck group would be trivial. To exclude genus one, the topological classification identifies X with the square torus; the explicit translation cover C->C/(Z+iZ) computes its fundamental group as Z² by the published universal-cover/deck theorem. Thus G would be abelian and noncyclic. But a commuting disc automorphism preserves the boundary fixed set of a nonidentity element. For a hyperbolic element, swapping its two fixed points conjugates it to its inverse and cannot commute; after conjugating fixed points to 0 and infinity in the half-plane, all commuting elements are positive real scalings z->az. For a parabolic element, conjugate its fixed point to infinity and it to z->z+1; commuting elements are real translations z->z+t. In either case a discrete subgroup of this one-parameter real group is cyclic: discreteness follows from proper discontinuity, and the elementary least-positive-element argument applies. This contradicts G=Z². Hence a compact disc quotient has genus at least two. The three cases exhaust all compact surfaces, proving both directions. AC is inherited through genus and uniformization, not introduced by the finite group calculation.
